intro: Meta dropped a bombshell today, launching its Muse Wonder AI models — and going closed-source to do it, signaling a dramatic break from its open Llama playbook just as the debate over open versus closed models heats up. Meanwhile, the AI world keeps reshuffling: Character.AI is filing for bankruptcy with Disney swooping in, the UAE is making AI a required school subject starting in kindergarten, and American Express is building guardrails to keep AI agents from going on unauthorized shopping sprees. It's a day that makes one thing clear — AI isn't just changing the tech industry anymore, it's rewriting the rules for education, finance, regulation, and everything in between.

stories.title: Meta launches Muse Wonder and Wonder Full AI models
stories.summary: Meta Superintelligence Labs released two new AI models, Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full (codenamed Watermelon). The models are available to Muse Code subscribers and via the Meta Model API, and Meta claims they rival leading competitors including OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra, Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5, and Claude Fable 5.1. Both models are closed-source, marking a departure from Meta's open Llama era. Meta plans to eventually power its Muse AI agent with Wonder, though no timeline has been provided.
stories.opinion: Meta's shift to closed-source frontier models signals a strategic reversal that prioritizes competitive positioning over the open-ecosystem philosophy that defined the Llama era. Whether Wonder Full's strong benchmark showings translate to real-world dominance remains to be seen. Where coverage differs: The Rundown AI reports Wonder Full scored 55 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, landing #2 behind Opus 5.5 (57) and ahead of Gemini 4 Argon, GPT-6 Astra, and Claude Fable 5.1 (all 53); The Verge references only Meta's internal benchmarks without specific scores The Rundown AI specifies Muse Code pricing at $50 or $200/month and notes API pricing below OpenAI and Anthropic's top tiers; The Verge does not mention pricing

stories.title: Harvard professor argues reading fiction builds better leaders for the AI age
stories.summary: Harvard Business School professor Sandra Sucher teaches MBA students moral leadership through novels, poems, and plays without AI assistance. UCLA professor Maryanne Wolf's neuroscience research supports the claim that deep reading strengthens critical thinking, empathy, and decision-making—skills the article argues become more valuable as AI handles routine information processing.
stories.opinion: A compelling case that the soft skills cultivated by literary engagement may be the hardest to automate—and therefore the most strategically important for future leaders to develop.

stories.title: Former UK attorney general warns AI faces less regulation than household appliances
stories.summary: Richard Hermer, former UK attorney general, argues that AI currently faces less regulatory oversight than ordinary household appliances like refrigerators. Drawing on national security experience, he calls for urgent public debate and robust application of international law, warning that existing governance frameworks are inadequate for the scale of AI's risks.
stories.opinion: The comparison to appliance regulation is attention-grabbing, but the piece is more a call to action than a policy blueprint—the harder question of what effective AI regulation looks like remains unanswered.

stories.title: 5th Circuit rules FedEx worker's harassment reports not protected under Title VII
stories.summary: The 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that a former FedEx Office employee's six harassment reports did not constitute protected activity under Title VII because the reported conduct—bullying, aggressive, and hostile behavior—was not sufficiently linked to a protected characteristic such as race. The court held that any adverse actions taken in response could not be classified as retaliation.
stories.opinion: The ruling underscores the importance of explicitly tying workplace complaints to protected characteristics when seeking Title VII protection, a nuance employees and HR departments alike should note.

stories.title: Meta design director shares how Muse AI agent was designed
stories.summary: Alex Cornell, design director at Meta, discusses Muse's design principles: treating AI conversations like human interactions, using progressive disclosure, keeping generative UI structurally fixed while varying content, and maintaining a single persistent chat thread as an ongoing relationship. He also shares personal AI workflows including turning Instagram saves into shopping catalogs.
stories.opinion: The emphasis on relationship-like interaction design rather than task-oriented UI reflects a bet that users will engage with AI agents more like companions than tools—a design philosophy with significant implications for retention and trust.

stories.title: MIT Technology Review weighs open AI models' benefits against their risks
stories.summary: The article examines whether open AI models' benefits outweigh their risks, prompted by Anthropic's report claiming Z.ai's openly available GLM-5.3 model poses cyberattack risks. It notes that commercial incentives shape both sides of the debate—Nvidia advocates for open models while Anthropic urges caution. Currently closed models remain more capable but open models trail by only months.
stories.opinion: The piece effectively surfaces how financial incentives color the safety debate on both sides, making it hard to take any company's position at face value without accounting for their business model.

stories.title: UAE becomes first country to mandate AI as a required subject from kindergarten through 12th grade
stories.summary: The UAE has become the first country to require AI as a subject across all K-12 grades, including kindergarten. Rather than giving young children generative AI tools, schools use role-play, storytelling, and guided discussions. Dubai's Knowledge and Human Development Authority is developing a 10-year roadmap for personalized, technology-integrated learning.
stories.opinion: The UAE's approach of teaching AI literacy through age-appropriate methods rather than direct tool access is a thoughtful middle ground in a global debate that too often frames the choice as all-or-nothing.

stories.title: American Express launches framework to prevent unauthorized AI agent purchases
stories.summary: American Express introduced an 'Intent Intelligence Framework' to ensure AI agents only make purchases users have explicitly authorized. The system captures purchase instructions via a Create Intent API, generates a unique Intent ID and Proof of Intent Token, and issues a secure digital payment credential for checkout instead of using actual credit card numbers. The framework is part of Amex's ACE Developer Toolkit launched in April 2026.
stories.opinion: As AI agents increasingly handle transactions, Amex is positioning itself as the trust layer between autonomous agents and consumer wallets—a smart strategic move that could set industry standards if widely adopted.

stories.title: Whole Foods wins summary judgment after catching plaintiff falsifying time records
stories.summary: A federal judge granted summary judgment to Whole Foods after security camera footage showed the plaintiff routinely left the facility immediately after clocking in, misrepresenting his work hours. The plaintiff had alleged race discrimination, retaliation, and FMLA violations, but the judge found the time falsification was legitimate grounds for termination and that the company had fired employees of various races for similar conduct.
stories.opinion: The case illustrates how documented evidence of policy violations can decisively undermine discrimination claims, reinforcing the importance of consistent enforcement and surveillance records for employers.

stories.title: AI labs increasingly buying data from defunct startups to train models
stories.summary: AI labs are purchasing code, emails, chats, and workspace data from failed startups through brokers like SimpleClosure and Sunset. SimpleClosure's Asset Hub has handled over 150 deals and expects to return over $10 million to startups by end of 2026. The trend emerged as AI labs hit limits of public and synthetic datasets, with buyers seeking authentic workplace interactions. Prices vary widely since valuations are based on speculative research theses about data utility.
stories.opinion: This emerging market turns startup failure into a data supply chain, but the lack of published benchmarks comparing real-world training data against alternatives means buyers are operating largely on faith.

stories.title: Character.AI files for Chapter 11 bankruptcy, agrees to sell assets to Disney for $20 million
stories.summary: Character.AI, the chatbot platform founded in 2021 by former Google engineers, has filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy. The company agreed to sell some assets to Disney for $20 million along with a non-exclusive perpetual license for its technology. The bankruptcy follows Google's $2.7 billion deal to license its models and poach its founders in 2024, multiple lawsuits related to child safety, and operational struggles to scale.
stories.opinion: Character.AI's rapid rise and fall—from unicorn to bankruptcy in under five years—is a cautionary tale about consumer AI companies that achieve massive user growth without a sustainable business model or adequate safety infrastructure.

stories.title: Texas logistics company pays $500K to settle EEOC claims of rejecting female applicants
stories.summary: Birchstone Management, a Texas-based logistics company, agreed to pay $500,000 to settle EEOC claims that it rejected female job applicants for pallet repairer positions since 2020, hiring men with similar or fewer qualifications. The settlement includes appointing an HR professional to revise hiring policies and conduct training.
stories.opinion: The case is part of a broader pattern of EEOC enforcement against employers who exclude women from physical labor roles, signaling that sex-based hiring assumptions remain a costly compliance risk.

tweet_headlines.headline: The co-founder of Moosend is building __MX Zero__, an analytics and campaign layer on top of SES and SendGrid — inspired by vibe-coders slashing newsletter bills from $4k to under $300.
tweet_headlines.source_text:
Last week, @marclou  vibe-coded a Beehiiv alternative and cut his newsletter bill from $4,000 a year to under $300.  

I couldnt stop thinking about this over the weekend. So I am thinking of building something.  

With AI, more people can build software that fits exactly how they work. I think we are seeing the dawn of the era of personal software. 

I co-founded Moosend. For ten years, I built exactly the kind of platform people are now walking away from. Sitecore acquired us in 2021.

Everyone can send emails with Amazon SES and Sendgrid. The problem with these tools is they come with no frills (no campaigns, or recipient tracking, location or email client analytics etc)

So I'm building the frills. It's called MX Zero.

MX Zero connects to SES, SendGrid or Postmark. It figures out what you're sending, then shows you the reporting you used to get from your email platform: opens, clicks and delivery for every campaign, by country, email client and day, down to each recipient.

Literally 30 seconds to your first dashboard.

So you can build your very own email marketing tool on top of SES and still get your fancy analytics back.

I'm gauging demand and will be onboarding in small batches.

Comment or DM me if you're interested and I'll move you up the waitlist. The link is in the first comment.

tweet_headlines.author: ericosiu
tweet_headlines.headline: Eric Siu screens AI-native hires with __six questions__, including how much of your tactical work AI does today and which products you've stopped using because of it.
tweet_headlines.source_text:
We're hiring AI-native people. If you apply, these are the six questions we'll send you.

Answer them well, and you move to the shortlist.

1. How many hours are you spending per week on X?
2. What percent of your tactical work is done by AI right now?
3. What is your daily AI driver, and how are you using it specifically?
4. How much are you spending out of pocket when it comes to AI?
5. What is the most impactful build you've made, and are you able to share it?
6. What workflows or products have you stopped using in the last six months?

Why these six:

• Hours on X: X is where the AI action is happening right now. It shows whether you're obsessed with learning this stuff.
• Tactical work done by AI: shows whether robots are doing the robot work, so you can do the human work.
• Daily driver: shows how deep your day-to-day use actually goes.
• Out of pocket: shows whether you're putting your own dollars behind it and investing in yourself.
• Best build: the rubber meets the road when you show what you've actually built and how you built it.
• Stopped using: this moves so fast that you have to keep eliminating as you add.

If that's you, apply. Link below.

human_items.headline: 5th Circuit rules FedEx worker's harassment reports not protected under Title VII
human_items.summary: The 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that a former FedEx Office employee's six harassment reports did not constitute protected activity under Title VII because the reported conduct—bullying, aggressive, and hostile behavior—was not sufficiently linked to a protected characteristic such as race. The court held that any adverse actions taken in response could not be classified as retaliation.
human_items.meaning: Be explicit about whose work changes and what happens to the people doing it.

human_items.headline: Whole Foods wins summary judgment after catching plaintiff falsifying time records
human_items.summary: A federal judge granted summary judgment to Whole Foods after security camera footage showed the plaintiff routinely left the facility immediately after clocking in, misrepresenting his work hours. The plaintiff had alleged race discrimination, retaliation, and FMLA violations, but the judge found the time falsification was legitimate grounds for termination and that the company had fired employees of various races for similar conduct.
human_items.meaning: Be explicit about whose work changes and what happens to the people doing it.
